Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!

The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.

“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”

If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.

Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.

At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.

As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.

Macroharder

SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.

Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.

“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement

SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.

On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.

Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.

The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger

Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.

Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.

Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money

Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”

Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.

Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.

From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:

It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.

It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?

The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”

Shares and shares alike

Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”

At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”

If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout

Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.

Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible.

What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.

What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner.

Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune.

So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

  • Elizabeth Lopatto

translation.html:
哦，当然，SpaceX 的信用风险相当高，因为它即将再借 400 亿美元购买 Nvidia 芯片，可谁在乎呢？SpaceX 和 Tesla 已经成立特别委员会，讨论合并事宜了！

你觉得这次合并有多吸引人，很可能取决于你有多相信 Elon Musk 想去火星的说法，或者用他在本周 SpaceX 财报电话会议上（以及此前的 S-1 文件中）的话来说，想要“传播意识之光”。但凡对情况有所了解的人都知道，我们还没有能让人类在太空生存的技术，坦白说，甚至连开发这种技术所需的基础信息都没有。因此，就得靠机器人。但地球与月球或火星之间的通信延迟，让控制机器人变得困难。所以下一步符合科幻逻辑的推演，就是让人工智能机器人只需地球提供极少的监督，就能自主作出决策。

“在开发超级智能软件方面开展合作，能带来很多好处。”

如果你相信 Musk 的说法，我们所说的这些技术，正通过自动驾驶汽车（Tesla）、大语言模型（SpaceX）和人形机器人（Tesla）来开发，而它们全都需要数据中心（SpaceX）。正巧，两家公司刚刚都公布了财报。另一方面，如果你认为火星只是 Musk 用来向公众解释自己种种出格举动的一套有用说辞，那么，这次合并能给他带来大量财富和控制权。

Musk 在最近的 SpaceX 财报电话会议上表示，将 SpaceX 和 Tesla “合并有很多好处”。为什么？“在开发超级智能软件方面开展合作，能带来很多好处。”但人工智能——啊，不好意思，是超级智能软件——其实并不是 SpaceX 目前真正的主营业务。在周二公布的第三季度财报中，SpaceX 报告称，人工智能——抱歉，抱歉，是超级智能部门的营收为 75.6 亿美元。其中，“SI 解决方案与基础设施营收”这一子类别——我认为这把 Grok、Cursor 和新型云服务业务打包算在了一起——跃升至 70 亿美元，是上一季度的三倍多。其中一部分来自把 Cursor 拼接进来，这带来了 6.08 亿美元营收。DA Davidson 分析师 Gil Luria 表示，这 70 亿美元中，其余部分很可能主要来自向 Anthropic 和 Google 出租算力；Grok 的贡献大概较少。

乍一看，这似乎能与 Anthropic 这类公司的营收相提并论。Anthropic 泄露的 S-1 文件显示，该公司今年上半年通过前沿模型获得了 163 亿美元营收。但 SpaceX 的 AI 业务看起来更像 CoreWeave，而非 Anthropic。虽然新闻稿告诉我们，“企业客户和消费者对 Grok 的采用有所增加”，但相关营收并未与裸金属服务器业务营收分开披露。而如果 Musk 想拿这个吹嘘，他肯定早就吹了。

至于周三公布第三季度业绩的 Tesla，财报糟透了，利润连续第二个季度下滑。原因在于，Musk 显然已经对普通汽车没那么感兴趣了。Tesla 转而专注于机器人，还有，我猜，自动驾驶出租车。（最近还做了一个 Roadster 跳跃汽车的演示，但那东西还得过几年才能投产，价格非常昂贵，而且 Tesla 无法保证会交付。）Musk 在 Tesla 的电话会议上没有进一步解释他关于合并的言论。

更硬的 Macrohard

SpaceX 和 Tesla 已经有一些业务往来；例如，SpaceX 就从 Tesla 购买了价值 1.31 亿美元、销量不佳的 Cybertruck。它过去也持有过 Tesla 债券。更关键的是，两家公司还共同宣布了两个 AI——去他妈的，我们就叫 AI 了——项目：Terafab 和 Macrohard。

Terafab 是 Musk 打算在得克萨斯州建设并运营的芯片制造项目，用来给自己供应芯片；Intel 算是在与 Musk 合作开发相关技术。Macrohard 则是，呃，一个让人们模拟 Microsoft 已有软件的 AI 项目。至少，我觉得它应该是干这个的。打出后者的名字，都让我祈祷小行星现在就撞过来把我们一锅端了，所以，自从 3 月宣布以来，我们就没怎么听说过它，或许也算幸运。

“Musk 过去设定的时间表，他旗下的公司多次未能兑现，”路透社指出。这种措辞的克制程度，我只能称之为带着冷幽默的轻描淡写

SpaceX 5 月的 S-1 文件称，Terafab 和 Microhard “尚处于非常早期的阶段，因此，我们与 Tesla 尚未敲定有关合作的诸多细节，包括但不限于财务条款、知识产权以及合作的最终期限”。截至本月早些时候，Intel 首席执行官仍表示，该公司继续致力于这项合作，但它没有义务继续参与 Terafab，而且 S-1 文件称，双方可能永远不会达成最终协议。我发邮件询问在此期间是否签署了任何协议，Intel 的 Thomas Hannaford 没有立即回复。

在本周与 SpaceX 投资者的电话会议上，Musk 声称 Terafab 将在 2028 年下半年实现量产。他还表示，公司将在 2027 年 5 月或 6 月拿到该工厂生产的首枚测试芯片。“Musk 过去设定的时间表，他旗下的公司多次未能兑现，”路透社指出。这种措辞的克制程度，我只能称之为带着冷幽默的轻描淡写。当电话会议上的一名分析师询问，Musk 是否已订购制造尖端设备所需的机器时，Musk 没有回答。

公司私下推进的事情，往往比公开宣布的更多，所以我不会把 S-1 申报文件视为完全定论。但最近一份 10-Q 季度报告没有提到 Macrohard，也没有提到 Terafab。

Matt Levine 支持 SpaceX 与 Tesla 合并的理由

Musk 肯定会拍着桌子大谈月球、火星“以及更远的地方”，而他的粉丝中有相当一部分人非常吃这一套。但股东可能也有一些比较无聊的财务理由，对合并抱有兴趣。

假设你天生就跟我很不一样，而且有钱得多，也因此持有不少 Tesla 股票。你非常信任 Elon Musk——显然如此——但你注意到，这个人的注意力跟嗑了可卡因的松鼠差不多。他基本上整天泡在 X 上，还经常发表种族主义言论。他老往白宫跑，干些惹恼 Tesla 潜在客户的事。然后，他又公开跟总统吵起来。有时候他对火箭兴奋不已，有时候对 Dogecoin 兴奋不已，有时候特别痴迷 Grok，有时候也会想想汽车。但你发现，不管怎么说，他最近花在汽车上的心思少多了。

基本上，你只要说一句“Nvidia”，就会有人给你一他妈大笔钱

既然他似乎正专注于 AI——如果他的状态也能叫专注的话——你就会注意到一些相当严重的利益冲突。长期观察 Musk 的 Matt Levine 指出，比如，Musk 旗下的公司“都需要同样稀缺的 Nvidia 芯片来驱动各自的 AI”。但如果把这些公司合并起来，或许就能打造出最好的通用 AI。然后呢？“如果你打造出了最好的通用 AI 模型，或许它既能开车、操作机器人、上传人脑，又能在 Twitter 上输出右翼观点。”

此外，眼下正在大规模建设 AI 基础设施，所以基本上，你只要说一句“Nvidia”，就会有人给你一他妈大笔钱。这次合并会把所有 AI 项目堆到一起，另外，我想，还有一些汽车、火箭和卫星。Levine 写道：“‘给我们 1000 亿美元，让我们在太空建设数据中心，但如果出于某种原因我们没建成，你们可以收走我们的汽车工厂和地面数据中心’，这对债权投资者来说是个不错的推介。”

Musk 也有建设实体基础设施的经历，尽管并非总能成功。至少在我看来，说到建设数据中心，把钱押在他身上，比押在转型而来的某些比特币矿商身上更靠谱。Luria 说：“如果 Elon 按照他所说的速度建设，他就会有大量富余产能，并且能够把其中很大一部分卖出去。”

Levine 写道，从这个角度看，SpaceX 和 Tesla 显然应该合并：

它们竟然是两家独立的公司，简直疯了！同一个人掌管着两家规模庞大、业务高度重叠的实体 AI 公司！这简直是利益冲突和繁文缛节的噩梦！干脆把它们合并，让这个人每天走进办公室时，只需要遵循一个简单的指令：作出能让这个庞大 AI 综合体及其股东的整体价值最大化的选择。如果某些芯片、工程师、钻机或其他什么东西应该用于机器人，那就去做机器人；如果应该用于数据中心，那就去做数据中心。股东都已经跟着他走到这一步了，想必信任 Musk 能作出这些决定。只是现在，做机器人对 Tesla 有利，对 SpaceX 不利；做数据中心对 Tesla 不利，对 SpaceX 有利。Musk 无法同时把两家的利益都放在首位。有个简单的解决办法。

当然，事情并没有那么简单。交易细节很重要；很多人都假设这会是一场换股合并。（“我猜收购方会是 SpaceX，部分原因是它的市值更高，但主要是因为 Musk 在那里的控制权更大，”Levine 写道。）监管环境同样重要。以 AI 为理由主张 SpaceX 和 Tesla 应该合并，这不也有点构成反垄断层面上不该让它们合并的理由吗？

当前的监管环境，姑且说是比较宽松，而这在很大程度上要归因于 Musk 通过 DOGE 亲信进行的干预。现任总统 Donald Trump 的任期还剩两年。此外，市场已经开始一波又一波地对 AI 感到不安。今年夏天早些时候，先有那桩 Situational Awareness 的事，接着又有最近那桩 CoreWeave 的事，所以，投资者情绪可能正在变化。这意味着，“各方正推动在 2027 年上半年之前宣布交易，以便在本届政府任内完成交割”，彭博社援引“知情人士”的话写道。

同股同权

Musk 对 SpaceX 的控制力比对 Tesla 更强。由于持有特殊的超级投票权股份，他的投票权超过 50%。他身兼首席执行官、首席技术官和董事长。股东能够通过法律途径挑战这种权力的空间非常有限。申报文件是这样表述的：“这将限制或使您无法影响公司事务及董事选举。”

但在 Tesla，Musk 只有约 20% 的投票权。（“只有”！）因此，在由 SpaceX 作为收购方的换股合并中，Musk 一下子就能获得整个合并实体的投票控制权。科罗拉多大学博尔德分校法学院教授 Ann Lipton 说：“他通过唯一可行的方式，获得了 Tesla 的投票控制权。既然 Tesla 已经上市，他就无法再把它改成双重股权结构。这是唯一的办法。”

如果 SpaceX 以 2 万亿美元或更高价格收购 Tesla，Musk 就能拿到一笔报酬

Lipton 表示，两家公司都设在得克萨斯州，这让股东很难提起诉讼。“无论是 Tesla 还是 SpaceX 的股东，能够起诉的可能性都微乎其微，因为得克萨斯州为股东诉讼设置了太多障碍。”这么一来，这项风险就没了。

先把更复杂的国家安全（涉及 SpaceX）和反垄断问题放到一边。Lipton 指出，在联邦层面，证券法主要问的是“你披露了吗？”所以，美国证券交易委员会，或者说这个机构剩下的那点人手，会希望看到所有信息都在投票前向股东披露。只要披露准确，也就这样了。在州层面，可能会有一些问题——因利益冲突而促成不公平交易，构成违反信义义务——但 Shari Redstone 的确让 Paramount 和 CBS 合并了，所以这并非不可能。

Musk 能从这次合并中得到什么？首先是控制权，这向来是他最爱的东西。根据彭博社的报道，这次合并还可能让他的净资产增加 1100 亿美元。但更有意思的是，合并会如何影响 Musk 在 Tesla 的巨额薪酬方案。如果发生法律意义上的控制权变更——例如 SpaceX 收购 Tesla——那么 Musk 那份巨额薪酬方案中的经营业绩里程碑条件就会失效。

届时，重要的就是 Tesla 的估值。如果 SpaceX 支付 2 万亿美元或更多，Musk 就能拿到一笔报酬。交易价格为 2 万亿美元时，Musk 将获得价值 60 亿美元的股票。他 2018 年薪酬方案中的股票也会加速归属，这些股票原本要到 2028 年才会归属。控制权变更还意味着，他可以更早出售这些股票。

这对 SpaceX 有好处吗？假设最终交易价格在 2 万亿美元或其附近，那么这基本上就是一场对等合并，意味着现有 SpaceX 股东的持股会被稀释得惨不忍睹。更糟糕的是，Tesla 的业务停滞不前，而它的 AI 雄心又十分烧钱。Shawn Tully 在《财富》撰文称：“SpaceX 和 Tesla 第四季度的合计资本支出，很可能会接近惊人的 500 亿美元，而它们的业务远远无法覆盖这笔开支。”

所以，单从数字来看，我倾向于认为，没什么好处，真的，对 SpaceX 并没有那么好。但说到底，Musk 的所有生意都不只是数字的问题，在某种程度上，它们取决于你有多相信 Elon Musk。Tesla 相对于传统汽车制造商的估值，从一开始就是这么回事。所以行吧，好吧，把它们拼起来，看看会发生什么。到了这个份上，愿意买 Musk 那套说辞的人，想必都知道自己答应参与的是什么。
